analysis.one_liner: Bans union membership or dues as a condition of employment nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a Senate vote and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal labor law so that no employer and union anywhere in the country could agree to require workers to join the union or pay dues as a condition of the job. Today, about half the states already have such 'right-to-work' laws; this bill would impose that rule nationally, including on railroad workers. Unions would still have to bargain for and represent every worker in a workplace, but workers could stop paying for that representation.
analysis.who_benefits: Individual employees who prefer not to pay union dues or fees, even when they are covered by a union contract, and employers who would no longer face union security agreements that strengthen union finances and membership.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the sections of federal law that let a union and employer sign a contract requiring employees to join the union as a condition of employment, so no worker anywhere could be required to join a union to keep a job.

It also strikes the provision letting railroad carriers require payroll deduction of union dues or fees as a condition of employment, ending that arrangement for railroad workers covered by the Railway Labor Act.
The bill's stated purpose is to protect each employee's freedom to choose whether to form, join, or assist a labor organization, or to refrain from doing so.

analysis.who_pays: Labor unions, which would lose dues and fee revenue from workers in their bargaining units who stop paying, weakening the money unions use to organize and bargain. Workers who count on union bargaining power would bear the indirect cost, since research on state right-to-work laws links them to lower wages and weaker union membership.

drawbacks.text: Federal law requires a union to represent every worker in a bargaining unit, union member or not; if workers can receive contract benefits without paying dues, unions lose revenue while keeping the same obligations, which critics say is designed to starve unions of the resources they need to organize and bargain.

Studies of state right-to-work laws generally find lower wages and union membership in right-to-work states, so opponents of this bill would argue that applying that rule nationwide would drag down pay for union-represented workers generally.

Supporters' strongest objection to the existing law is the reverse: a worker can currently be fired for refusing to join a union or pay fees under a union security agreement, and this bill is meant to end that compulsion.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The individual freedom argument — no worker should be forced to join or pay a union to keep a job — is sincere and the bill does what it says. But the mechanism depends on workers being able to opt out of paying while unions remain legally required to represent them, and the consistent finding from states with such laws is weaker unions and lower pay for the workers those unions represent. The bill offers nothing to offset that; its practical effect would be to shrink union finances and bargaining power nationwide.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar in its first week, and then it simply sat there — no committee, no hearing, no floor vote — until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jim DeMint introduced the bill on May 3, 2007, with four Republican cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice in its first two days and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 132, on May 4, 2007.
No committee is listed for the bill and the action history shows no hearings, no markup, no floor debate, and no vote after it was placed on the calendar.
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill died with it, never having received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Labor unions and the workers whose pay and conditions depend on union bargaining are better off, since a national ban on union security agreements never came close to a vote. Employers who would have benefited from weaker union finances gained nothing because the bill died.

for.name: Sen. Jim DeMint
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Right-to-Work Act and got it placed on the Senate calendar.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; the record shows no action after the bill was placed on the calendar.

against.name: AFL-CIO and organized labor
against.what_they_did: Consistently opposed national right-to-work legislation, which unions view as an effort to cut off their dues base.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all four cosponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic majority that controlled the Senate never took the bill up; there is no sign of Democratic support in the record.

industries.note: The bill would end union security agreements nationwide, letting workers in union contracts skip dues while unions must still represent them. That cuts the dues revenue unions rely on to organize and bargain, which is why union and worker interests in defeating this bill ran together.

Employers would no longer bargain with unions whose membership and finances are secured by the contract, weakening union leverage at the table. The benefit to employers comes directly out of workers' collective bargaining strength.

The bill strikes the Railway Labor Act provision allowing carriers and unions to agree to payroll deduction of dues as a condition of employment, a special rule that covered railroad workers. Rail carriers would gain a freer hand; railroad unions would lose a long-standing arrangement.
